lesson.title: Locking Cells Together: The Three Jobs of Cell Junctions
lesson.summary: Cell junctions are specialized protein structures that connect animal cells to their neighbors or to the extracellular matrix, and different junction types are built to seal tissues, anchor them mechanically, or let cells communicate directly.
lesson.body:
A sheet of epithelial cells lining the gut or the skin has to do something that a single free-floating cell never has to manage: hold together as a coherent barrier while its cells stay physically and chemically connected to their neighbors. That job falls to cell junctions, specialized protein complexes built into and around the plasma membrane that fall into three functional categories, each doing something the plasma membrane alone cannot do on its own.

The first category is about sealing. Tight junctions form a continuous band of fused proteins, largely a family called claudins, that circles each cell near its apical surface and welds it to its neighbors, closing off the space between cells so that fluid cannot leak freely through the gaps. This is why the lining of the small intestine can control exactly what gets absorbed into the body: molecules have to pass through the cells themselves, using specific transporters in the plasma membrane, rather than slipping between them.

The second category is about mechanical anchoring, and it connects directly back to the cytoskeleton. Desmosomes are spot-like junctions where cadherin proteins from neighboring cells bind to each other in the space between the cells, while on the inside of each cell those cadherins are anchored to a plaque that intermediate filaments, typically keratin in epithelial cells, attach to. This creates the exact tissue-wide mechanical network described earlier: a shock delivered to one skin cell is distributed across the whole sheet rather than tearing a single cell apart. Adherens junctions do a related job using cadherins linked instead to the actin cytoskeleton, and they are often found as a continuous belt near the apical surface, helping a tissue change shape during development by coordinating actin-based contraction across many cells at once. Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane, part of the extracellular matrix, using integrins rather than cadherins, tying this junction category directly to the matrix discussed previously.

The third category is about communication. Gap junctions are clusters of channel proteins called connexins, six of which assemble into a ring called a connexon on one cell's membrane, which docks with a matching connexon on the neighboring cell to form a continuous pore connecting the two cytoplasms. Ions and small molecules can pass directly through, letting electrical signals spread rapidly between cells, which is exactly how cardiac muscle cells coordinate a heartbeat: an electrical impulse spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions so the heart contracts as one coordinated unit rather than as thousands of independently firing cells.

These three junction types are not mutually exclusive. A single epithelial cell in the intestinal lining typically has tight junctions near its apical surface, adherens junctions and desmosomes below that providing mechanical integrity, and gap junctions scattered along its lateral surface for communication, an arrangement that echoes the same core themes running through this whole set of concepts: cells resist mechanical stress using cytoskeletal cables, connect to a supporting matrix, and, whether through plasmodesmata in plants or gap junctions in animals, find ways to stay in direct cytoplasmic contact with their neighbors.
